note.specFocus: Why family life matters to Christians, and debates about religious upbringing and family responsibilities.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.7 Family Structures and Responsibilities
Family is seen by most Christians as the primary place where faith, values and love are first taught and experienced.
Passing on faith
• Deuteronomy 6:6–7 instructs parents to teach God's commandments diligently to their children, "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way" — showing the family's central role in religious education long before formal church teaching.
• Ephesians 5–6 sets out household codes describing mutual duties within families: love between spouses, children honouring parents, and parents raising children "in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4).
• Infant baptism, godparents and family worship are practical ways Christian families commit, from a child's earliest life, to nurturing their faith.
Family structures and roles
• Christian views on gender roles within the family vary: some more traditional Christians see distinct, complementary roles for men and women; many other Christians support full equality between spouses in family decision-making and responsibilities.
• Family responsibility also extends to caring for elderly or vulnerable relatives, which many Christians see as an extension of the commandment to honour one's parents (Exodus 20:12).
Debates about religious upbringing
• Many Christians see bringing children up in the faith as a loving duty that gives children identity, moral grounding and community.
• Humanists and some liberal thinkers argue children should be free to explore beliefs and decide for themselves once old enough, cautioning against indoctrination.
Exam link: "Evaluate" answers on religious upbringing should weigh parental duty/community support against concerns about a child's freedom to choose — not just assert one side.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Deuteronomy 6:6–7 instructs parents to teach God's commandments diligently to their children, "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way", showing that the family is traditionally seen as the first and most important place where faith is passed on.

Second, Ephesians 5–6 sets out mutual duties within the household, including love between husband and wife and the honouring of parents by children, so family relationships are understood as part of living out Christian faith in daily life, not separate from it.

Finally, Through practices such as infant baptism, saying grace, family prayer and attending church together, family life gives children a direct experience of Christian community and values, helping the next generation to grow in faith.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Many Christians argue that Ephesians 6:4 instructs parents to "bring [children] up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord", which they see as a parental duty rather than an optional choice, since faith shapes moral values and gives life meaning.

A second consideration is: Through infant baptism, godparents and the wider church community formally commit to supporting a child's religious upbringing, showing that it is viewed as a shared responsibility that benefits both the child and the community.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Humanists and some liberal religious thinkers argue that children should be allowed to explore different beliefs and decide for themselves once they are old enough to understand the choice, rather than being taught one religion as if it were simply true.

A further consideration is: Critics of compulsory religious upbringing argue it can amount to indoctrination if children are not also exposed to other viewpoints, and that good moral character and a sense of purpose can be developed without religious belief, for example through Humanist approaches to ethics.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: this often depends on whether religious upbringing is seen primarily as passing on loving guidance and identity, or as limiting a child's freedom to form their own beliefs. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of love, nurture, parental responsibility, baptismal promises and the Church as a wider family and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
